provider: iCloud Keychain and Google Password Manager

Q12.value: failure mode observed. After quitting and reopening the browser, an assertion scoped to the stored non-discoverable credential id was offered only over the cross-device path (a phone QR), with no on-device Touch ID option. Forcing the internal transport then returned NotAllowedError and Safari reported no local passkey for the origin, so there was no on-device copy to use. A user without a second device could not authenticate. Confounders: dozens of passkeys for one origin and user, mid-test fingerprint-set changes, and a cache clear. The earlier fresh single-session runs did assert locally with stable bytes, so persistence of the secret holds, but reliable on-device re-assertion after a restart did not.

Q13.value: demonstrated more strongly than the formal clear-site-data test. The identical PRF output 712f0c24...e05ea5 appeared in both Firefox and Safari on the same Mac, two different browser profiles, so the credential and its PRF secret live in iCloud Keychain outside any single browser profile. Clearing one browser's site data cannot remove a credential another browser already reads

Q11a.value: WebAuthn creation is impossible inside a dedicated worker, PublicKeyCredential is undefined there. Confirmed on every browser row

Q11b.value: topology viable. The HKDF key imported from the PRF bytes survived a structured-clone transfer into a worker (key survived transfer=true), the worker derived with it (worker derived=true), and raw export failed in both the page and the worker (non-extractable). Derived bits 6a9b02ed48a9e2b344afd51a7d55fd2bdd1a49e12bf66863555f00f6b8600640

notes: Durability. Q13 (credential lives outside the browser profile) is proven by cross-browser byte identity, the strongest form. Q12 surfaced a real failure mode rather than a clean pass: after a browser restart the platform passkey was offered only cross-device (QR), and forcing on-device transport gave NotAllowedError with no local passkey shown, so a user without a second device could be locked out. This is the risk the operator flagged. It is confounded by heavy test churn (many same-user passkeys, fingerprint changes, cache clear) and does not reproduce the earlier clean single-session Touch ID asserts, so it is a risk to design against, not a proven everyday breakage. The PRF secret itself is persistent (synced passkey), the issue is the browser's willingness to offer the local credential after a restart. Q11 topology fully answered: creation cannot happen in a worker (Q11a), but a derived CryptoKey survives transfer to a worker, is usable there, and is non-exportable (Q11b), so the browser design has a viable worker topology.

browser: Android System WebView (Chrome 150 wv), in a minimal WebView app

A5.value: confirmed: the WebView has no WebAuthn. PublicKeyCredential is undefined, so passkeys and the PRF extension are unavailable. navigator.credentials exists (create and get are present, the password/federated surface) but the public-key part is absent, so navigator.credentials.create with a publicKey option cannot work. isSecureContext=true because it loaded over localhost via adb reverse, so this is a real WebView limitation, not an untrustworthy-origin false negative

notes: A5 measured directly in a real Android System WebView on the SM-M526BR, not inferred from compat data. Raw check: {hasPublicKeyCredential:false, hasCredentials:true, hasCredentialsCreate:true, hasCredentialsGet:true, isSecureContext:true}. Consequence: an app rendering in a WebView (how a shipping Dioxus Android app renders via wry) cannot use the browser WebAuthn PRF gate. Blitz/dioxus-native also omits WebAuthn by design, so either Dioxus rendering path forces the native Android Keystore route (A6) for a gate, or none.

A6.value: set_user_authentication_required(true) gates the key. Using it without a fresh authentication was refused (the Keystore threw), which is the gate. The ungated key (flag false) stored and read a secret with no prompt

notes: A6 gates as expected, the Android counterpart of macOS N3, so Android needs no upstream work on the flag itself and is ahead of Apple where the equivalent flag is absent from keyring. Important sub-finding: the stock android-keyring 0.2.0 default credential path hardcodes set_user_authentication_required to false, so a plain keyring::Entry is NOT gated. Getting a gate means building the key yourself with the flag set (what this probe does). A full prompt-driven read past the refusal is the app's BiometricPrompt plus CryptoObject job, out of scope here. Provenance: android-keyring is a single-author dependency. Built by hand with NDK 28 (no Gradle) and run on the SM-M526BR. This closes the Dioxus-app question: since a WebView has no WebAuthn (A5), the native Keystore gate (A6) is the viable route, and it works.

notes: I1: iCloud Keychain supports PRF on the iPhone via Face ID, stable 32 bytes. CONFIRMED Apple PRF derivation model: the PRF is a function of (iCloud account, user id, input), independent of rp.id and of the specific credential instance. Evidence, all on one device and account: different user id gives different output (Q7: 712f0c24 vs 399d7bee), while different rp.id with the same user id gives the identical output (Q7b: pippo.tail0b5119.ts.net and tail0b5119.ts.net both 712f0c24). Credential dependence in the spec's sense holds (different credential via different user id differs), but RP does not isolate keys. Contrast Google Password Manager, which is per-credential-instance (two same-user same-RP passkeys differ, 1eee0139 vs 4a07cb40). Design consequence: on Apple a fixed user id yields one shared key across every site for that Apple account, so keys must be diversified by user id or input salt, never assumed unique per site or per credential. This is an iCloud Keychain behavior, so it applies to macOS Safari too (the cross-device macOS-localhost equals iPhone-ts.net match is consistent).
